analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give full cash refunds for canceled COVID-era flights instead of vouchers.
analysis.headline: The bill requiring cash refunds for canceled pandemic flights drew 46 Democratic cosponsors but never got a committee vote before Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: During the COVID-19 emergency, travelers who canceled trips or whose flights were canceled were often offered vouchers or credit instead of their money back. This bill would have required large airlines and ticket agents to promptly offer a full cash refund, including fees, for any ticket for a covered flight, with the choice to take a voucher instead. It also let passengers who had already accepted a voucher swap it back for cash, and allowed airlines to use some COVID relief money to pay those refunds.
analysis.who_benefits: Travelers who paid for flights on large carriers that were canceled during the pandemic, or who canceled their own tickets. They would get their cash back promptly, including ancillary fees, rather than being steered into vouchers that expire or lock them into flying the same airline later. Passengers who had already accepted vouchers could convert them back to cash.

how_it_helps.text: Requires large passenger airlines (over $1.5 billion in 2018 revenue) and foreign carriers flying US routes, plus ticket agents, to promptly offer a full cash refund, including ancillary fees, for any canceled ticket during the emergency period, whether the airline or the passenger canceled it [S2][S3].
Lets airlines offer vouchers as an alternative, but only if the voucher never expires and the offer clearly tells passengers of their right to cash [S2][S3].

Allows passengers who already received a voucher before the bill became law, and had not used it, to exchange it for a cash refund, and requires ticket agents to be promptly reimbursed by the airline [S2][S3].
Permits airlines to use COVID relief appropriations to fund the refunds, while barring use of the CARES Act payroll-support funds that were tied to keeping workers employed [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large passenger airlines, which would have to pay back billions in fares they had collected and largely settled in vouchers or credit, either from operating cash or other COVID relief funds (not the dedicated payroll-support grants). Ticket agents would front refunds but get reimbursed by the carriers.

drawbacks.text: The refunds would land on airlines at the moment of deepest crisis: demand had collapsed and carriers were burning cash, so forcing prompt cash payouts could worsen industry losses and, in a worst case, push weaker carriers toward layoffs or bankruptcy [S3].

The bill allows airlines to cover refunds with COVID relief appropriations other than the payroll-support program, meaning public relief dollars would partly subsidize the payouts rather than the airlines bearing the full cost [S3].

The rules apply only to carriers with more than $1.5 billion in 2018 operating revenue and only to flights touching US airports during the defined emergency period, leaving smaller carriers and later-period flights outside the requirement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For travelers the upside is direct and substantial: real money back for trips that never happened, with vouchers as a genuine choice rather than the only option. The honest cost is that airlines absorb a large payout during a revenue collapse, softened somewhat by allowing relief funds other than payroll grants to pay for it. The narrowest carriers are exempt, but that exemption barely touches the passengers with the most money at stake.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and an aviation subcommittee from May 2020 onward and never reached a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Steve Cohen introduced the bill on May 22, 2020, with 21 original cosponsors [S3].
It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the House Financial Services Committee on the day of introduction [S5].
Four days later it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Aviation, and no further action was recorded [S5].
Forty-six House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored, and neither committee ever took it up before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The major passenger airlines, which kept passengers' money in vouchers and credit instead of paying out cash refunds, are better off because the bill never moved. Airlines had accepted roughly $25 billion in federal payroll support in the same period, which the bill specifically barred from funding refunds.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Major airlines kept fares as vouchers

for.name: Steve Cohen
for.role: Representative from Tennessee and bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Cash Refunds for Coronavirus Cancellations Act and recruited cosponsors

for.name: 46 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican did

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took up or marked up the bill; it sat there and in the Aviation Subcommittee until the Congress ended

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the referred bill without any recorded action for the rest of the Congress

against.name: Airlines and their trade groups
against.what_they_did: Pressed to settle cancellations with vouchers and credit rather than cash refunds, the practice this bill would have overridden

sides.party_line_note: All 46 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on, but the bill never reached a vote, so how members would have split on the floor is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have forced large carriers to hand back billions in fares as cash rather than vouchers during the pandemic, drawing on relief funds other than the dedicated payroll grants. Vouchers kept the airlines' cash while transferring the risk to travelers; cash refunds reverse that.

industries.industry: Travel and online booking agencies (ticket agents)
industries.note: Agents would have to pass refunds through to customers quickly, a short-term cash strain, but the bill entitles them to prompt reimbursement from the airlines for the airline's share, so the lasting cost falls on the carriers.
